title: Understanding the Role of Multisensory Design in Museums to Enhance Visitors’ Experience with Language Barriers: A Case Study of Islamic Museums in Makkah, Saudi Arabia
content: The increasing diversity of museum visitors is driven by globalisation, migration, and re-ligious tourism, posing pressing accessibility challenges, particularly language barriers. Museums in Makkah, as pivotal sites of Islamic heritage, attract millions of visitors of var-ying linguistic backgrounds annually. This research examines the effects of multisensory elements (visual, auditory, tactile, and olfactory) on visitor comprehension, spatial en-gagement, and satisfaction in the presence of language barriers. Employing a mixed-methods approach, this study begins with a quantitative analysis and examines the role of multisensory elements in the visiting experience using a multilingual survey of 321 international visitors. This is followed by examining the association between these ele-ments and the probability of revisiting the museum to understand a visitor’s behavioural intention to revisit the museum. Finally, a thematic analysis of the open-ended questions was used to identify the pros and cons of using multisensory elements in museums. The findings validate that tactile experience is demonstrated to be a significant predictor of re-visit intention, but auditory experience is not found to be significant. Crucially, the adapted anthropological concept of embodied piety, defined here as the active cultivation of spiritual and historical connection through disciplined physical and sensory engage-ment, emerged as a culturally resonant framework distinct from Western ocular-centric models. However, implementation must balance immersive design with spatial autonomy to mitigate sensory overload and technology usability barriers. Success requires culturally sensitive, co-created spatial design that accommodates diverse cultural scripts regarding physical contact and public interaction. Strategically integrated multisensory design func-tions as a non-linguistic interpretive pathway, enhancing comprehension, engagement, and inclusion for linguistically diverse visitors to Islamic heritage sites, with pronounced cultural variation requiring curatorial calibration rather than monolithic approaches.
